correctness.rationale: The classical simple ordered prolate modes identify the top normalized sinc eigenfunction with the no-node Sturm–Liouville mode. In unweighted Lebesgue normalization F_c^*F_c=(2π/c)K_c; differentiating the sinc kernel gives the cosine kernel divided by π. The finite-Fourier equation at x=1 and Hellmann–Feynman therefore give Λ'=2Λb/c. The smooth simple differential eigenfunction branch in L² is also smooth up to the endpoints, by expressing it as F_c applied to the branch divided by its nonzero Fourier eigenvalue. Its endpoint value does not vanish: if it were zero, pψ'(x)=−∫_x^1(qt²−χ)ψ(t)dt would bound |ψ'| by a constant times the supremum of |ψ| on a short endpoint interval; integrating would force ψ to vanish there. For q=c², differentiating the differential equation gives W'= (x²−m_q)ψ², with W(0)=W(1)=0 by evenness, normalization/mean, and endpoint regularity. The integrand changes sign once, so W<0 in 0<x<1. Thus ∂_q log(ψ_q(x)/ψ_q(1))=−∫_x^1 W/(pψ_q²)>0 for x<1; the quotient has a finite endpoint limit since W vanishes linearly and ψ_q(1)>0. Differentiating the squared normalized ratio integral explicitly gives ∂_q(1/b)>0, not just weak monotonicity. Also 0<χ<=q/3 and the same single-sign-change argument applied to (pψ')' gives ψ strictly decreasing spatially, hence 0<b<1/2. Differentiating Λ' then gives strict concavity for every c>0.
